strengths: Introduces a well-motivated new task (interaction-aware RVOS) addressing a genuine gap in existing RVOS benchmarks, which largely treat referred objects in isolation without modeling actor-target relationships.

InterRVOS-8K is large in scale (127K expressions, 8.7K videos) with a high object-per-video ratio and explicit actor-target pair annotations, filling a niche not covered by prior datasets such as MeViS, ReVOS, or Ref-SAV.

The four-stage automated annotation pipeline (object description -> single/multi referring expressions -> interaction detection -> interaction-aware expression generation) is clearly described and the prompts are provided in the appendix, aiding transparency.

ReVIOSa's actor/target special-token design ([SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR]) is a reasonable and simple extension to existing SAM2+MLLM segmentation frameworks, and the paper provides an ablation (Table 6) showing the benefit of joint versus independent token supervision.

Experiments span multiple axes: cross-dataset training comparisons (Ref-SAV vs InterRVOS subsets), per-caption-type breakdowns, zero-shot generalization to MeViS/Ref-YoutubeVOS/Ref-DAVIS, and qualitative examples, providing a fairly comprehensive empirical picture.
The proposed actor-target-aware evaluation protocol is a useful complementary metric for probing interaction understanding specifically, beyond aggregate J&F scores.
weaknesses: The dataset's core value rests entirely on automatically generated (GPT-4o/LLaMA-70B) captions and interaction/role labels, yet the paper reports no human verification, annotator agreement, or quality/error-rate analysis of the pipeline's outputs (e.g., correctness of unidirectional vs bidirectional classification, actor/target role assignment accuracy). This is a significant gap given that the entire contribution hinges on data quality.

The evaluation set itself is constructed via the same automatic pipeline (with filtering to boost interaction-centric samples), so any systematic errors or biases in caption/mask generation likely propagate into the benchmark used to score all models, undermining the reliability of reported comparisons.

It is not clearly explained how pixel-level segmentation masks are derived from VidOR (which provides bounding boxes, not masks) — this critical annotation detail for ground-truth mask tracks is missing or unclear.

Baseline comparisons are relatively narrow: the main quantitative comparison is against Sa2VA (upon which ReVIOSa is directly built), Referformer, and LMPM; more recent MLLM-based segmentation methods cited in the related work (e.g., VideoGLaMM, VISA, ViLLa) are not benchmarked, making it harder to assess how much of the gain is attributable to the proposed architecture versus the underlying MLLM+SAM2 backbone.

The architectural novelty is incremental — extending a single [SEG] token to a pair of [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens is a fairly straightforward modification of existing LISA/Sa2VA-style token-prompted segmentation, rather than a substantially new modeling approach for relational reasoning.

The video clip extraction procedure (selecting only first/last 1000-frame bins and truncating to 500 frames) appears somewhat arbitrary and could bias the dataset toward specific temporal segments of long videos, potentially limiting temporal diversity.

Performance on interaction expressions specifically is noted to be lower than other categories (Table 4), and while attributed to the need for architecture improvements, this is not deeply analyzed with error cases or ablations isolating why interaction reasoning remains harder.

The paper's actor-target-aware evaluation depends on expressions where the correct actor/target split is unambiguous, but for interactions involving 3+ objects (noted as 20.3% of interactions), the actor-target framing may be an oversimplification, and this complexity is not thoroughly discussed or evaluated.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and novel task extension to RVOS: explicit actor-target role separation for interaction expressions, which addresses a genuine gap in existing RVOS literature that treats interactions as single-object or grouped-motion segmentation.

Contributes a large-scale automatically annotated dataset (InterRVOS-127K, 127K expressions, 8.7K videos) that is substantially larger than prior datasets and uniquely provides actor-target mask pairs; the four-stage annotation pipeline (object description, expression generation, interaction detection with directionality, and role-aware expression synthesis) is clearly described and includes human refinement of the evaluation set.

Proposes a reasonably simple and effective architectural extension (dual [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens plus attention mask loss) that is compatible with existing MLLM+SAM2 pipelines, with ablations showing complementary contributions of each component (+2.6 for tokens, +1.5 for AML, +5.0 combined).

Extensive supporting analysis in the appendix, including layer-head selection rationale for AML, attention correlation studies motivating the loss, qualitative visualizations, and zero-shot/cross-dataset comparisons showing InterRVOS-127K provides good data efficiency and transfer versus Ref-SAV/ReVOS.

Reasonable performance gains are shown not only on the new InterRVOS-Actor/Target split but also on standard RVOS benchmarks (MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS), suggesting the approach is not narrowly overfit to the new benchmark.
weaknesses: The dataset is fully automatically generated using GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B captioning plus SAM2 mask tracks, with only the evaluation set receiving human correction; there is no reported quality metric (e.g., human agreement, annotation error rate) for the training set or a rigorous quantification of the evaluation-set correction process, raising quality concerns for a dataset contribution positioned as a primary contribution.

Baseline comparisons for the new InterRVOS-Target setting are essentially only against the paper's own model variants, since prior methods are described as inherently incapable of producing a target mask; this makes the 'state-of-the-art' claim for interaction-aware segmentation somewhat vacuous without a naive baseline (e.g., prompting existing models twice with actor-focused and target-focused phrasings) to isolate the true benefit of the proposed architecture.

The evaluation protocol details (e.g., how ground-truth actor/target roles are matched to model outputs, how errors in the model's own interaction-vs-non-interaction decision affect scoring) are not fully specified in the main text, which could materially affect interpretation of the reported J&F improvements.

The architectural novelty is somewhat incremental (token duplication plus an attention-supervision auxiliary loss), and the paper does not compare against a simpler baseline isolating whether gains stem from additional supervision signal (more masks/loss terms) versus a qualitatively different interaction understanding.

It is unclear how multi-object interactions (up to 20.3% involve three objects per the dataset statistics) are handled within the binary actor/target framework used for both annotation and evaluation.

Presentation is dense with heavy reliance on the appendix for essential experimental details (e.g., standard RVOS benchmark comparisons, zero-shot results, prompt templates), somewhat undermining the self-containedness of the main paper.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and novel task (InterRVOS) that identifies a genuine gap in standard RVOS: most existing methods collapse interaction expressions into a single referred object, ignoring the asymmetric actor/target roles that are semantically central to describing many video events.

Proposes a large-scale (127K expression) automatically annotated dataset with a carefully designed four-stage pipeline (object appearance/motion extraction, single/multi-instance expression generation, interaction detection with directionality, and interaction-aware expression generation) that is clearly documented with prompts and examples in the appendix.

The architectural contribution (dual [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens plus attention mask loss) is simple, technically sound, and well-motivated by an empirical analysis showing correlation between attention concentration on object regions and segmentation quality (Appendix B.1).

Extensive ablations and analyses: layer/head selection study for AML, supervised vs. non-supervised head comparisons, per-component ablation (Table 4), and zero-shot generalization experiments across multiple standard RVOS benchmarks (Appendix C.2-C.3), lending good support to the claims.

Strong empirical results: ReVIOSa outperforms strong existing MLLM-based baselines (Sa2VA, VideoLISA, VISA) on both interaction-aware and standard RVOS settings despite comparable or smaller model sizes, and the dataset itself is shown to be more sample-efficient than a comparable automatically-annotated dataset (Ref-SAV).
Good presentation: clear figures illustrating the task, pipeline, architecture, and attention visualizations aid understanding and reproducibility of the core ideas.
weaknesses: Because the dataset is fully automatically annotated (GPT-4o + LLaMA-70B) except for the manually refined evaluation set, the paper provides no quantitative measure of annotation quality/accuracy for the training data (e.g., human audit of actor/target role correctness, interaction directionality accuracy, or caption faithfulness), leaving open the possibility of systematic labeling noise that is hard to detect from downstream metrics alone.

In Table 2, the InterRVOS-Target column can only be compared against the paper's own two model variants (ReVIOSa-1B/4B) since no baseline supports target segmentation; this makes the 'state-of-the-art' claim on InterRVOS-Target somewhat vacuous as a comparison, since there is no independent point of reference for what a reasonable target-segmentation score should be.

The layer-head selection strategy for AML (top-1 layer, top-4 heads) is derived empirically per model without a principled justification for why this specific configuration generalizes, and the paper does not discuss sensitivity/robustness of this choice across different backbones or training runs beyond the 1B/4B cases shown.

The video clip extraction procedure (only first and last 500-frame bins of long source videos) is an ad hoc heuristic that could bias the dataset toward particular scene types or interaction moments, and its effect on dataset diversity/quality is not analyzed.

Some standard-RVOS benchmark comparisons mix models of different scales and base LLMs (e.g., 7B/13B vs. the proposed 1B/4B), which somewhat complicates fair attribution of gains to the proposed method versus base model capacity, though the paper does partially address this by noting ReVIOSa's smaller size.
